name: Woodhenge and the Durrington Walls Southern Circle
about: Two Late Neolithic timber monuments 2 miles north-east of Stonehenge, rebuilt from their excavated postholes. Woodhenge: six concentric oval (egg-shaped) rings of postholes, lettered A (outer) to F (inner) by Maud Cunnington, who dug the whole interior in 1926-28; the long axis points roughly to the midsummer sunrise; a child's grave lay near the centre; a ditch with an external bank and one north-east entrance surrounds the rings; the timber rings are dated about 2600-2450 BC and the henge earthwork somewhat later; at least two sarsens were set on the south side later. Nothing above ground survives: the Cunningtons marked the postholes with concrete markers (not exactly on the post positions) and the grave with a flint cairn; the bank and ditch are ploughed almost flat. The Southern Circle, inside the south-east entrance of the great henge of Durrington Walls about 60-70 m north of Woodhenge, was dug by Wainwright in 1966-67 (about two-thirds; the western third left unexcavated) and again by the Stonehenge Riverside Project in 2005-06: a Phase 1 of four rings of slender posts with a central four-post setting and a south-east facade, replaced in Phase 2 by six rings of massive posts with a south-east entrance between two huge posts facing the midwinter sunrise, a platform before it, and a 170-180 m avenue running to the River Avon on the midsummer sunset line. Nothing survives above ground (the A345 road crosses the site). The henge of Durrington Walls (bank about 440-500 m across) is context only; under its bank lay a ring of large posts, first announced in 2015 as buried standing stones, shown by excavation in 2016 to be postholes. Research file: quotes are exact text from the cited pages (whitespace and OCR as fetched); values read from table images are marked derived.

indicating that both that monument and Woodhenge are more likely to have been free-standing structures.

debate.claim: 'Stonehenge for the ancestors' (Parker Pearson and Ramilisonina 1998): timber at Durrington for the living, stone at Stonehenge for the ancestors, linked by the Avon and the two avenues; contested by Wainwright and Darvill.

cites.quote: The main theory that has motivated our own project is that Stonehenge was built for the community’s ancestors (Parker Pearson and Ramilisonina 1998a)
He suggests that the timber circle at Durrington Walls represented life and a land of the living, whilst Stonehenge and the down around it, encircled by burial mounds, represented a land of the dead.
Geoff Wainwright and Timothy Darvill have contested Pearson's theories, however.

The orientations of the circles and their avenues, together with seasonality patterns of pig culling, show that the midwinter and midsummer solstices were important times for gathering at these sites.

Originally the ditch was 5.5 metres (18 ft) deep, 7 metres (23 ft) wide at its bottom and 18 metres (59 ft) wide at the top.
The bank was in some areas 30 metres (98 ft) wide.

entrances.value: north-west and south-east (possibly also south and north-east)

cites.quote: There were two entrances through the bank and ditch – at the north western and south eastern ends.

post_ring_under_bank.what: 2015: geophysics read as a buried row of up to 90 standing stones (some up to 4.5 m) under the southern bank; 2016 excavation found postholes with ramps whose posts had been lifted out and the holes filled with chalk rubble before the bank was built. Popular estimates of the posts: about 300 trunks, about 7 m high (Wikipedia), up to 5 m high and 3 tonnes (trail booklet) - not from the excavation report.

cites.quote: has now discovered evidence for a row of up to 90 standing stones
The hidden arrangement of up to 90 huge standing stones formed part of a C-shaped Neolithic arena
But the excavation team uncovered two pits for wooden posts.
“They have got ramps at the sides to lower posts into,” said Nicola Snashall
Excavation in 2016 showed that the geophysical anomalies recorded by the SHLP are postholes, not stone sockets.
The ring of around 300 huge trunks stood on the same line where the Durrington Walls outer bank now stands.
Each trunk was approximately 1.5 metres (4 ft 11 in) in diameter and 7 metres (23 ft) high
These huge tree trunks may have been up to 5 metres high, and weighed up to 3 tonnes each.

plans.title: Woodhenge on-site bronze plaque 'Plan of Rings' (photograph)
plans.licence: Photograph CC BY-SA 3.0 (Wikimedia Commons). The plaque was one of the Cunningtons' bronze and enamel plaques (stolen 2015); if drawn by the Cunningtons (Maud d. 1951, Ben d. 1950) its design is public domain in the UK since 2022, but the plaque's designer is not stated: check before tracing.
plans.what it shows: all six rings of Woodhenge coloured by ring, ramps of rings B and C, north arrow and a scale bar in feet (0-160 ft); taken almost square-on, so traceable with a perspective correction against the scale bar. Shows the excavated posthole plan, not the concrete markers.

plans.title: Cunnington 1929, Woodhenge, general plan
plans.licence: Public domain in the UK if drawn by Maud Cunnington (died 1951; life + 70 years ended 31 Dec 2021); no scan found online (not on the Internet Archive, Google Books or HathiTrust).
plans.what it shows: the original survey of every posthole, ditch sections and the extra holes; the best source to trace if a scan can be obtained (Wiltshire Museum, Devizes, holds the Cunnington archive).

plans.title: Wainwright with Longworth 1971: fig. 85 Plan of Woodhenge (p. 208); figs. 9, 11, 12, 14 Southern Circle general plan, Phase 1, Phase 2 and post-pipe positions; Appendix VIII posthole details
plans.licence: (c) Society of Antiquaries of London; ADS terms of use, not an open licence: use to check positions, ask the Society before tracing.
plans.what it shows: fig. 14 plots the post-pipe (actual timber) positions of Phase 2; Appendix VI gives the ring centres; the western third of the circle is unexcavated.

plans.title: Gaffney et al. 2020, A Massive, Late Neolithic Pit Structure associated with Durrington Walls Henge (Internet Archaeology 55)
plans.what it shows: survey maps of the Durrington Walls henge and its surroundings: usable to place the henge bank and Woodhenge (not checked for a plan of the Southern Circle).

gaps: Historic England pages refuse scripts (403): the scheduling entry, the Research Records and, most importantly, Marshall, Chadburn et al. 2024, 'Woodhenge, Durrington, Wiltshire: radiocarbon dating and chronological modelling' (Research Report 94/2024), and Ruggles and Chadburn 2024, Stonehenge: sighting the sun, with Sharon Soutar's plan and the measured solstitial axes. Only Chadburn's summary in The Past was quotable.

Cunnington 1929 (Woodhenge) is not online; per-posthole positions, diameters and depths for Woodhenge are only available as Wainwright's ring averages (Table XXI) and the 1930 review. The 1930 review (62 posts in ring A) and Wainwright (60) disagree; neither sums to the 168 posts of Wikipedia and Chadburn.

Riverside Project results for the Southern Circle (Trenches 7 and 19, 2005-06), the Woodhenge stone holes (2006 'cove') and the 2016 posthole excavation under the bank are in Stonehenge Riverside Project Volume 3 (Durrington Walls and Woodhenge: a place for the living, Sidestone, forthcoming 22 April 2027, CC BY-NC-ND). Thomas 2007 (internal features, BAR) and Parker Pearson et al. 2007 Antiquity were not reachable openly.
No measured azimuth for the Southern Circle entrance or the Durrington avenue was found in a fetchable source; only the henge entrance axis (123 deg 30') and the solstice statements.
No grid reference or coordinates for the Southern Circle itself; it must be placed from Wainwright's figs. 2-3 (27.4 m NW of the east entrance) or the Internet Archaeology maps.

Post heights are estimates only (7.5 m, 24 ft, 6 m for Woodhenge; 10.5 m roof only on the roofed reading for the Southern Circle); no source gives heights per ring. Height above ground could be estimated from posthole depth, but no quoted rule was found.
Phase 1 ring counts of the Southern Circle are uncertain (presumed numbers '?' and '?44' in Table I).
